question: What are Spring bean scopes?
title: Spring Bean Scopes Overview
direct_answer: Bean scope defines how many instances of a bean Spring creates and how long they live. The five scopes are: singleton (default — one per context), prototype (new per injection), request (one per HTTP request), session (one per HTTP session), application (one per ServletContext).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know all five bean scopes and can explain when each is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning singleton and prototype, forgetting the three web scopes (request, session, application)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton problem and how Spring uses proxies to handle web scopes injected into singletons

sections.title: Understanding Spring Bean Scopes
sections.content: **Bean scope** controls the lifecycle and visibility of Spring-managed objects. Think of it like rental agreements: singleton is buying one car that everyone shares, prototype is renting a fresh car each time you need one, and web scopes are like valet parking — you get your specific car back during your restaurant visit (request) or your entire membership period (session). Spring's default is **singleton** because most business logic classes are **stateless** — they don't hold user-specific data, so sharing one instance across all requests is safe and memory-efficient. The **prototype** scope creates a new instance every time the bean is requested, useful for stateful objects like form commands. The three **web scopes** (request, session, application) tie bean lifecycle to HTTP constructs and require a web-aware ApplicationContext. Understanding scopes prevents subtle bugs: injecting a prototype into a singleton doesn't give you fresh instances unless you use special techniques like **ObjectProvider** or **scoped proxies**.

sections.title: Declaring Different Bean Scopes
Key Points
content: **Singleton scope**: one instance per ApplicationContext, shared by all dependents, default for all beans unless specified otherwise
**Prototype scope**: new instance created every time the bean is requested via injection or getBean(), Spring does not call PreDestroy on prototype beans
**Request scope**: one instance per HTTP request, destroyed when response completes, requires web ApplicationContext
**Session scope**: one instance per HttpSession, survives across multiple requests from same user, perfect for user-specific state like shopping carts
**Application scope**: one instance per ServletContext, shared across all sessions and requests, similar to singleton but servlet-aware
**Scoped proxies**: required when injecting shorter-lived scopes (request, session) into longer-lived beans (singleton), Spring creates a proxy that delegates to the current scope instance

**Prototype-in-singleton trap**: injecting a prototype bean into a singleton via constructor or field injection only creates one prototype instance, use ObjectProvider or lookup methods for fresh instances

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Bean scope defines how Spring manages the lifecycle and number of instances for a bean. There are five scopes total. Singleton is the default — Spring creates one instance per ApplicationContext and shares it everywhere that bean is injected. This works great for stateless services like your typical at-Service or at-Repository classes. Prototype scope creates a brand new instance every time you request the bean, which you'd use for stateful objects like command objects or anything holding user-specific data that shouldn't be shared. Then there are three web scopes. Request scope gives you one instance per HTTP request — it's created when the request starts and destroyed when it ends. Session scope gives you one instance per user session, so it survives across multiple requests from the same user, perfect for things like shopping carts or user preferences. Application scope is one instance per ServletContext, shared across the entire web application. One gotcha that catches people: if you inject a prototype bean into a singleton using normal at-Autowired, you only get one prototype instance created when the singleton is built, not a fresh one each time. You need to use ObjectProvider or the at-Lookup annotation to get truly fresh prototype instances. For web scopes injected into singletons, you must set proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS so Spring wraps it in a proxy that delegates to the correct request or session instance.

A stateful ReportBuilder that accumulates data during processing needs a fresh instance per use. Web apps need beans tied to HTTP request or session boundaries. question: What is the singleton bean scope in Spring?
title: Spring Singleton Bean Scope
direct_answer: Singleton is the default scope — Spring creates exactly one instance per ApplicationContext and shares it wherever the bean is injected. It's ideal for stateless service classes like at-Service and at-Repository. Note: singleton scope is per context, not per JVM.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the most commonly used scope and its boundaries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying singleton means one instance per JVM — it's actually one per ApplicationContext, so multiple contexts can have separate singleton instances

sections.title: Singleton Scope in Spring
sections.content: **Singleton** is Spring's default bean scope, meaning Spring creates exactly **one instance per ApplicationContext** and reuses it for all injection points. Think of it like a shared office printer — everyone in the office uses the same machine. This is different from the Gang of Four singleton pattern, which enforces one instance per JVM classloader. Spring's singleton is per **container**, so if you have multiple ApplicationContexts (like in integration tests), each context has its own singleton instance. Singleton scope is the right choice for **stateless beans** — objects that don't hold request-specific or user-specific data. Your typical `@Service`, `@Repository`, and `@Controller` classes are stateless: they orchestrate business logic using injected dependencies but don't maintain internal state that changes between requests. This makes them inherently **thread-safe** when multiple HTTP requests execute concurrently. Singleton scope is memory-efficient and fast: Spring initializes the bean once at startup, and every injection gets a reference to the same object with zero overhead.

sections.title: Singleton Bean Example
Key Points
content: **One instance per ApplicationContext**: singleton scope is container-scoped, not JVM-scoped, so multiple contexts can have separate singleton instances
**Default scope**: all beans are singleton unless you explicitly declare another scope with at-Scope annotation
**Eager initialization**: singleton beans are created when the ApplicationContext starts up by default, not lazily on first use
**Thread safety requirement**: singleton beans must be stateless or use proper synchronization because multiple threads access the same instance concurrently in web applications
**Stateless design**: perfect for services, repositories, controllers that hold no request-specific or user-specific data in instance fields
**Immutable dependencies**: singleton beans can safely hold references to other singleton or prototype beans injected via constructor
**Memory efficient**: one instance serves all requests, eliminating the overhead of creating and garbage collecting instances per request

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Singleton is the default scope in Spring, meaning Spring creates exactly one instance of the bean per ApplicationContext and reuses that instance everywhere it's injected. So if you have an at-Service class, Spring builds one instance when the context starts and injects that same instance into every controller or other service that needs it. It's important to know that singleton here means one per Spring container, not one per JVM — if you have multiple ApplicationContexts running, like in integration tests, each context gets its own singleton instance. Singleton scope is perfect for stateless beans, which is most of your business logic classes. A stateless bean doesn't hold any request-specific or user-specific data in its fields — it just orchestrates operations using its injected dependencies. This makes it inherently thread-safe because there's no mutable state that multiple threads could corrupt. For example, your OrderService might have a placeOrder method, but it doesn't store order data as an instance variable — it receives the order data as method parameters and uses repositories to persist it. One thing to watch out for: if a singleton bean holds mutable state in instance fields that get modified during requests, you'll have race conditions when multiple requests execute concurrently. That's why the singleton default works — Spring assumes you're writing stateless services, which is the correct design for web applications.

question: What is the prototype bean scope and when do you use it?
title: Spring Prototype Bean Scope
direct_answer: Prototype scope creates a new bean instance every time it's injected or requested via getBean(). Use it for stateful beans, command objects, or any bean where sharing an instance would cause correctness issues. Spring does NOT call PreDestroy on prototype beans.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when singleton scope is inappropriate and prototype is necessary
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Spring doesn't manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans — no PreDestroy callback is invoked
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton trap and all three solutions: ObjectProvider, at-Lookup method injection, and ApplicationContext.getBean()

sections.title: Prototype Scope and When to Use It
sections.content: **Prototype scope** tells Spring to create a **brand new instance** every time the bean is requested — either through injection or via `ApplicationContext.getBean()`. Think of it like disposable coffee cups: you get a fresh one each time, not a shared mug. This is the opposite of singleton, where everyone gets the same instance. Use prototype for **stateful beans** — objects that hold data specific to one use case and shouldn't be shared. Examples include form backing objects, command objects in a command pattern, or any bean where concurrent use of the same instance would cause data corruption. A critical detail: Spring hands you the prototype instance and then **stops managing it**. Spring does NOT call `@PreDestroy` methods on prototype beans because it doesn't track them after creation. You're responsible for cleanup. Another gotcha: if you inject a prototype into a singleton via `@Autowired`, you only get one prototype instance (created when the singleton is built), defeating the purpose. You need **ObjectProvider**, `@Lookup` method injection, or manual `getBean()` calls to get fresh instances.

sections.title: Prototype Bean Declaration and Usage
Key Points
content: **New instance per request**: Spring creates a fresh bean instance every time you ask for it via injection or getBean(), no instance is ever reused
**Stateful beans**: prototype scope is for beans that hold use-case-specific data in instance fields that shouldn't be shared across requests or threads
**No PreDestroy callback**: Spring does not call at-PreDestroy methods on prototype beans because it doesn't track them after creation, you're responsible for cleanup
**Prototype-in-singleton trap**: injecting a prototype into a singleton via at-Autowired only creates one instance when the singleton is built, not fresh instances per use
**ObjectProvider solution**: inject ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean> into singletons and call getObject() each time you need a fresh instance
**Lookup method injection**: annotate an abstract method with at-Lookup and Spring generates an implementation that returns a fresh prototype each call
**Manual getBean()**: call applicationContext.getBean(PrototypeBean.class) to explicitly request a new instance, useful when ObjectProvider doesn't fit

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Prototype scope means Spring creates a completely new instance of the bean every time it's requested, either through injection or by calling getBean() on the ApplicationContext. You'd use prototype for stateful beans — objects that hold data specific to one operation and shouldn't be shared. A good example is a command object that processes one order. It holds the order details in instance fields while it's working, so if two threads shared the same instance, they'd overwrite each other's data and corrupt the processing. With prototype scope, each thread gets its own fresh instance. One critical thing: Spring doesn't call at-PreDestroy on prototype beans. Once Spring creates the instance and hands it to you, it stops tracking it. So if your prototype bean holds resources that need cleanup, you're responsible for that. The big gotcha is the prototype-in-singleton trap. If you inject a prototype bean into a singleton using normal at-Autowired, Spring only creates one prototype instance when it builds the singleton, and that singleton holds a reference to it forever. You don't get fresh instances. To fix this, you have three options. First, inject ObjectProvider of the prototype type and call getObject() every time you need a new instance. Second, use at-Lookup on an abstract method and Spring generates an implementation that returns a fresh prototype each call. Third, manually call applicationContext dot getBean() whenever you need a new instance. ObjectProvider is usually the cleanest approach.

question: What are request and session scopes in Spring?
title: Request and Session Scopes in Spring
direct_answer: Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request — bean is created when the request starts and destroyed when it ends. Session scope creates one bean instance per HTTP session — lives for the user's session lifetime. Both require proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS when injected into singletons.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand web-specific scopes and how they differ from singleton and prototype
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that proxyMode is required when injecting request or session scoped beans into singleton beans, causing startup errors
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a realistic session scope example like shopping cart or user preferences, and explain how the scoped proxy delegates to the current request or session instance

sections.title: Request and Session Scopes in Web Applications
sections.content: **Request scope** and **session scope** are web-aware scopes that tie bean lifecycle to HTTP constructs. **Request scope** creates one bean instance per HTTP request — when a request arrives, Spring instantiates the bean, and when the response completes, Spring destroys it. Think of it like a notepad you use during a phone call and throw away when you hang up. **Session scope** creates one bean instance per HTTP session — it survives across multiple requests from the same user until the session expires. Think of it like a customer's account page that remembers their preferences across visits. Both scopes require a **web ApplicationContext** (Spring Boot auto-configures this). A critical requirement: when you inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton, you MUST set `proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS`. Without it, Spring tries to inject the actual bean at context startup, but there's no active request or session yet, causing an error. The proxy wraps the bean and delegates to the correct instance at runtime.

rows: Created per HTTP request, destroyed after response
Created per HTTP session, destroyed when session expires
Request-specific tracking, correlation IDs, request context
User-specific state: shopping cart, preferences, authentication
Accessed by multiple requests from same user, needs synchronization
ShoppingCart with list of items for one user

sections.title: When to Use Request vs Session Scope
sections.content: Use **request scope** when you need to track information for the duration of one HTTP request. Common examples: a request correlation ID for logging (generate a UUID when the request starts, include it in all log messages, discard it when the request completes), request timing metrics, or a bag of request-specific context data that multiple services need to access. Request-scoped beans are inherently thread-safe because each request runs in its own thread with its own bean instance. Use **session scope** when you need to maintain state across multiple requests from the same user. Classic examples: shopping cart (user adds items across several requests, checkout on the final request), user preferences (theme, language, page size), or form wizards (multi-step forms where each step is a separate request but they share accumulated data). Session-scoped beans can be accessed by multiple requests from the same user, so if you modify shared mutable state, you need synchronization. For stateless authentication (JWT tokens), you typically don't need session scope — the token carries all state. But for traditional server-side sessions with HttpSession, session scope is perfect.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Request scope lifecycle**: bean created when HTTP request starts, destroyed when response is sent, perfect for request-specific context like correlation IDs
**Session scope lifecycle**: bean created on first access in a session, destroyed when session expires or is invalidated, ideal for user-specific state like shopping carts
**proxyMode required**: must set proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS when injecting web scopes into singletons, otherwise Spring throws an error at startup
**Scoped proxy mechanism**: Spring creates a CGLIB proxy that implements the bean's class and delegates method calls to the current request or session instance at runtime
**Thread safety difference**: request-scoped beans are single-threaded, session-scoped beans can be accessed by multiple concurrent requests from the same user
**Web context requirement**: both scopes require a web-aware ApplicationContext, automatically provided by Spring Boot when spring-boot-starter-web is on the classpath
**Cleanup**: Spring automatically calls at-PreDestroy on request and session scoped beans when the request or session ends, unlike prototype beans

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Request scope and session scope are web-specific scopes that tie bean lifecycle to HTTP concepts. Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request. When a request comes in, Spring instantiates the bean. When the response is sent, Spring destroys it. You'd use request scope for things like a request correlation ID — generate a UUID when the request starts, log it with every operation during that request, and discard it when the request completes. Session scope creates one bean instance per HTTP session. It lives for the entire time a user is interacting with your app, surviving across multiple requests until the session expires. Classic example is a shopping cart. The user adds items across several requests, and all those requests share the same session-scoped ShoppingCart bean. When the user logs out or the session times out, Spring destroys the bean. One critical requirement: when you inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton, you must set proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS in the at-Scope annotation. Without this, Spring tries to inject the actual bean when building the singleton at startup, but there's no active request or session yet, so it fails. The proxyMode tells Spring to create a CGLIB proxy that wraps the bean. At runtime, when you call a method on the injected bean, the proxy delegates to the correct instance for the current request or session. It's transparent to your code — you just call methods normally and Spring handles routing to the right instance behind the scenes.

question: What is the problem with injecting a prototype bean into a singleton in Spring?
title: Prototype Bean in Singleton Problem
direct_answer: When a prototype bean is injected into a singleton via at-Autowired, the prototype is only created once (when the singleton is created). The singleton holds a reference to this single prototype instance forever, effectively making it behave like a singleton. This defeats the purpose of prototype scope.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of how Spring resolves dependencies and the interaction between different scopes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming that because a bean is marked prototype, Spring will magically create new instances even when injected into a singleton, which it doesn't
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all three solutions: ObjectProvider for programmatic access, at-Lookup for method injection, and ApplicationContext.getBean() for manual retrieval

sections.title: The Prototype-in-Singleton Problem
sections.content: The **prototype-in-singleton trap** is a subtle bug where you declare a bean as prototype scope, inject it into a singleton, and expect to get fresh instances — but you don't. Here's why: when Spring builds a singleton bean at startup, it resolves all its dependencies **once**. If one dependency is prototype-scoped, Spring creates one instance of that prototype and injects it into the singleton via constructor or field. The singleton now holds a **permanent reference** to that single prototype instance. Every time the singleton uses the prototype, it's using the same instance, forever. The prototype effectively becomes a singleton. This defeats the purpose — you marked it prototype because you wanted fresh instances per use, but Spring's dependency injection happens once at construction time. The root cause is the **lifecycle mismatch**: singletons live for the entire ApplicationContext lifetime, prototypes should be created on demand, but the injection happens eagerly. Think of it like giving someone a disposable coffee cup once at the start of the day — they'll reuse that same cup all day instead of getting fresh ones.

sections.title: Problem and Solution with ObjectProvider
Key Points
content: **Root cause**: singleton beans are created once at startup and their dependencies are injected once, so a prototype dependency becomes a permanent reference
**Lifecycle mismatch**: singletons live for the entire ApplicationContext lifetime, prototypes should be created on demand, but normal injection happens eagerly
**ObjectProvider solution**: inject ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean> and call getObject() each time you need a fresh instance, cleanest approach for most cases
**Lookup method injection**: annotate an abstract method with at-Lookup and Spring generates an implementation that returns a new prototype per call, useful for callback-style APIs
**ApplicationContext.getBean()**: manually call applicationContext.getBean(PrototypeBean.class) to request a new instance, gives full control but couples your code to Spring
**Scoped proxy alternative**: set proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS on the prototype bean, Spring creates a proxy that delegates to a fresh instance per call, but rarely used for prototype
**Detection**: this bug is silent — no errors, no warnings, just wrong behavior where shared state causes data corruption across operations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The problem is that when you inject a prototype bean into a singleton using normal at-Autowired or constructor injection, Spring only creates one instance of the prototype — when the singleton itself is being constructed. The singleton holds a reference to that one prototype instance forever. Every time the singleton uses the prototype, it's using the same instance, so the prototype effectively becomes a singleton. This defeats the whole point of prototype scope, which is to get a fresh instance every time. The root cause is a lifecycle mismatch. Singletons are created once when the ApplicationContext starts up and live for the entire lifetime of the application. When Spring builds the singleton, it resolves all its dependencies at that moment. If one of those dependencies is a prototype, Spring creates one instance and injects it. That's the only time the prototype is created. After that, the singleton just keeps reusing it. There are three solutions. First and most common: inject ObjectProvider of the prototype type instead of the prototype itself. ObjectProvider is like a factory — you call getObject() on it every time you need a fresh prototype instance, and Spring creates one for you. Second solution is at-Lookup method injection. You declare an abstract method that returns the prototype type, annotate it with at-Lookup, and Spring generates an implementation that creates a new prototype each time you call it. Third solution is to inject the ApplicationContext and manually call getBean() whenever you need a prototype. This works but couples your code more tightly to Spring. ObjectProvider is usually the cleanest approach.

items: Wrong pattern: @Autowired TaskProcessor processor in a singleton — one prototype instance for the singleton's lifetime.
ObjectProvider fix (recommended): inject ObjectProvider<TaskProcessor> and call getObject() each time you need a fresh one.
@Lookup fix: annotate a protected abstract method — Spring overrides it to return a new prototype on every call.
ApplicationContext.getBean() fix: works but it's the Service Locator anti-pattern — avoid in production code.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, TaskService is singleton. TaskProcessor is @Scope("prototype") because it holds per-task mutable state. If TaskService @Autowires TaskProcessor directly, every task shares the same processor — state from task A bleeds into task B. The fix: inject ObjectProvider<TaskProcessor>. Each call to processorProvider.getObject() creates a brand new TaskProcessor. candidates miss: @Lookup also works — you declare protected abstract TaskProcessor createProcessor(); and Spring generates an implementation that creates a fresh prototype each time.

items: The bug is silent — Spring doesn't warn you that the prototype is being degraded to singleton behavior.
Don't use ApplicationContext.getBean() as the fix in your service layer — it's the Service Locator anti-pattern and makes testing harder.

speakable_v2.cap: Direct @Autowired of a prototype into a singleton silently breaks prototype semantics — always use ObjectProvider or @Lookup to get a fresh instance.

question: What is the default scope for Spring beans and why?
title: Why Singleton Is the Default Spring Bean Scope
direct_answer: Singleton is the default because most Spring beans are stateless services where sharing an instance is safe and efficient. Creating a new service instance per injection would waste memory and initialization time. Singleton is the correct choice for any stateless bean.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the design rationale behind Spring's defaults, not just memorizing that singleton is default
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not being able to articulate why singleton was chosen over prototype as the default scope
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect statelessness to thread safety in a multi-threaded web server environment where many requests execute concurrently

sections.title: Why Singleton is Spring's Default Scope
sections.content: Spring chose **singleton as the default** because the vast majority of beans in a typical enterprise application are **stateless services** — objects that orchestrate business logic without holding request-specific or user-specific data in instance fields. A stateless `@Service` or `@Repository` receives inputs via method parameters, performs operations using injected dependencies, and returns results, all without maintaining internal state that changes between calls. Since there's no state to corrupt, sharing one instance across all consumers is **safe and efficient**. Creating a new instance per injection would waste memory (hundreds of identical service objects in the heap) and waste initialization time (re-executing constructor logic, re-injecting dependencies). Singleton scope gives you **instant dependency injection** with zero runtime overhead — every `@Autowired` field or constructor parameter gets a reference to an existing object. In a web server handling hundreds of concurrent requests, this means all requests share the same `OrderService` instance, which is thread-safe as long as the service is stateless. If prototype were the default, you'd need to explicitly mark 95% of your beans as singleton, inverting the effort.

sections.title: Stateless Singleton Service Example
Key Points
content: **Stateless services dominate**: typical enterprise apps are mostly stateless services (at-Service, at-Repository, at-Controller), making singleton the right default for 95% of beans
**Memory efficiency**: one shared instance uses far less heap memory than creating new instances per injection point or per request
**Initialization cost**: singleton beans are constructed once at startup, avoiding repeated constructor execution and dependency wiring overhead
**Thread safety assumption**: singleton default assumes beans are stateless, which makes them inherently thread-safe in multi-threaded web servers
**Inversion of effort**: if prototype were default, you'd explicitly mark most beans as singleton, wasting time and cluttering code with scope annotations
**Spring philosophy**: convention over configuration — default to the most common case, allow explicit configuration for exceptions
**Stateful beans are rare**: beans that need per-use instances (command objects, form backing beans) are the minority, justifying prototype as the opt-in exception

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Singleton is the default scope because most beans in a typical Spring application are stateless services, and for stateless beans, sharing a single instance is both safe and efficient. A stateless service like OrderService or PaymentService doesn't hold any request-specific or user-specific data in its instance fields. It receives inputs via method parameters, performs operations using its injected dependencies, and returns results. Since there's no internal state that changes between method calls, multiple threads can safely call methods on the same instance concurrently without any risk of data corruption. This makes singleton the correct choice for the vast majority of beans. If Spring defaulted to prototype scope instead, you'd be creating a brand new instance of every service for every injection point. That's a huge waste of memory — imagine hundreds of identical OrderService instances sitting in the heap. It's also a waste of initialization time because each instance needs its constructor run and its dependencies injected. With singleton, Spring creates one instance at startup, and every at-Autowired injection just gets a reference to that existing object — zero runtime overhead. In a web application handling hundreds of concurrent requests, all those requests share the same singleton service instances. This works perfectly as long as the services are stateless. The few cases where you do need per-use instances — like command objects or form backing beans that hold operation-specific data — are the exception, not the rule. That's why prototype is opt-in. Spring's philosophy is convention over configuration: default to the most common case and let you explicitly configure the exceptions.

beats.text: Singleton is the default Spring bean scope because the vast majority of Spring beans are stateless service objects. A stateless bean has no mutable instance fields — it receives inputs through method parameters and returns outputs without storing anything. For stateless objects, sharing one instance across all callers is completely safe and dramatically more efficient than creating a new instance for every injection or request.

Web servers handle hundreds or thousands of requests per second. If every request created a new UserService, that's thousands of object allocations per second, each with dependency injection, followed by garbage collection. Singleton eliminates all that overhead for beans where sharing is safe.

items: Stateless bean: no mutable instance fields — only final dependencies set in the constructor. Safe as singleton.
Memory efficiency: one instance shared by all callers vs one instance per caller per request.
Initialization cost: constructor and @PostConstruct run once at startup, not once per request.
Stateful bean: has mutable instance fields that differ per use — needs prototype scope.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, OrderService has two final fields: UserRepository and EmailService, both set in the constructor. The service methods take an Order parameter and return an OrderResult. There's zero per-request state stored in the object. Sharing one OrderService instance across all requests is perfectly safe — and it means Spring creates it once at startup instead of once per request. sharp edge: the moment you add a non-final mutable field to a singleton — say private List<Event> pendingEvents — you've created a concurrency bug. Two threads adding to the same list will corrupt each other's data.

items: Don't store mutable per-request data in singleton fields — it's a concurrency bug waiting to happen under load.
Don't assume all beans should be singleton — stateful objects like command builders or accumulators genuinely need prototype scope.

speakable_v2.cap: The rule is simple: no mutable instance state means singleton is safe and efficient — any mutable state signals you need a narrower scope.
